# Communities creating change

## Authors

- Bridget M Kuehn<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-8783-4419](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8783-4419)) †

### Affiliations

1. eLife Chicago United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Women scientists across India are working together to build and advocate for family-friendly policies at their institutes.

## Support systems

There is a common thread that runs through the stories of Indian women scientists, according to Nandita Jayaraj, who created the website The Life of Science with fellow journalist Aashima Dogma in 2016. Those who succeed “have a really solid support system,” says Jayaraj.

Having a supportive spouse is essential. “Society as a whole has not changed on the time scale that [government and institutional] policies are changing,” explains Vidita A. Vaidya, a professor in the department of biological sciences at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Mumbai. “It’s a very patriarchal society. Women are the primary care givers, and women’s careers are always secondary to men’s careers.”

However, more men, especially younger men, are sharing childcare duties. When her children were very young, Maria Thaker, an assistant professor at the Indian Institute of Science’s Centre for Ecological Sciences in Bengaluru, often took them along for field studies. Now that the children are in school, she and her husband, who is also an ecologist, coordinate their work so that one stays with the children while the other heads to the field. “We feel like Superman and Clark Kent," says Thaker, “because we can’t be in same place at the same time.”

Some of Thaker’s male colleagues are also very engaged parents. Her department has adopted family-friendly policies; for example, they hold all meetings before 4:30pm to allow parents to pick up their children.

In addition, it is still common for the older generation to play an important day-to-day role in supporting families with children, according to Vaidya, who also serves on the Women in Science panel. She has her parents and in-laws nearby to help look after her child, and also has access to on-site childcare at TIFR.

But not all women are so lucky. Those who live farther from their families may face a dearth of childcare options, especially for infants. Hiring a nanny may be a financially viable option in India, but many parents prefer a childcare center, says Vaidya.

At the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research in Pune, Mayurika Lahiri, an associate professor of biology, has been instrumental in establishing an on-campus childcare center. It is so popular that it now serves 50 children of staff, faculty, and students. In 2008, when no such facility existed, Lahiri was able to arrange space on campus for a nanny to watch her infant daughter. It took six years to open an on-campus crèche. Lahiri’s department director created a childcare committee, on which Lahiri served, that interviewed daycare providers and selected the best fit. The institute provided the space and start-up funds for furniture and other materials, and now the fees paid by parents cover the day-to-day operating expenses of the facility. Lahiri shared her tips for starting a center with The Life of Science so others could follow in her footsteps.

“It gives me peace of mind,” says Lahiri, who sends her daughter to the center. “It gives you time to concentrate on your work or teaching.”

## Stopping the clock

Outdated institutional policies can also hold back women in their careers. “Our major problem in this country is having enough women in decision-making positions to be able to change attitudes and approaches,” says Visweswariah. However, this is not stopping existing senior women faculty from pushing for sensible solutions to the career challenges that mothers face in gaining tenure, landing jobs, or juggling childcare responsibilities.

Thaker sought help from Visweswariah and other biology division chairs at the Indian Institute of Science, who happened to be mostly women, after her application for tenure had a disappointing outcome. She was the first woman to be considered for tenure under a new process. The all-male panel who assessed Thaker did not factor in her six-month maternity leave, and compared her against a male colleague who had more publications. The result was that she received a three-year contract extension instead of tenure.

In response, Visweswariah and her colleagues successfully lobbied for an Institute-wide policy that provides mothers with more time to build their case for tenure without being penalized for having children. Women faculty can now ‘stop the tenure clock’ for one year per child, with a maximum of a two-year extension. For example, if a woman with two children gets tenured after seven years, her tenure and associated pay increase will be retroactively applied as if she was promoted at the end of her fifth year.

Pausing the tenure clock accounts for both the time spent on maternity leave and the time spent on infant care and nursing after returning to work. Visweswariah explains it takes some time to adjust after a child is born. “It’s not that you produce a child and then everything suddenly just disappears,” says Visweswariah. “I think male colleagues fail to understand that.”

Similar battles are taking place across India, as women try to secure places to breastfeed, promote hiring two-career couples, and support other policies that can help women stay in science. Improvements would happen faster, says Vaidya, if the government required such policies at all the institutions it funds: “These policies should not have to be reinvented every single time in every single institution all over the country.”

In the meantime, having a supportive community pushing for change is helping women stay the course. “When my colleagues in India and abroad rallied for me, I knew that I had to find a way to get past the administrative hurdles,” says Thaker. “Having a supportive community of colleagues makes all the difference.”

## Note

This Feature Article is part of the Scientist and Parent collection.

results.result: Successful women scientists in India rely on strong support systems including supportive spouses and multigenerational family support. While India remains a patriarchal society where women are primary caregivers and their careers are secondary to men's, there is a gradual shift with younger men increasingly sharing childcare duties.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 and C14 are based on expert opinions and general observations without quantitative data or systematic evidence. The characterization of Indian society (C4-C6) and the trend toward shared childcare (C7) lack empirical support such as survey data, demographic studies, or statistical analysis. These are qualitative assessments that may reflect individual perspectives rather than rigorously documented findings.

results.result: Maria Thaker and her ecologist husband coordinate their work schedules to manage childcare responsibilities, with her department implementing family-friendly policies such as scheduling all meetings before 4:30pm. Some of her male colleagues are also engaged parents.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C13 provide specific, verifiable examples of work-family coordination strategies and institutional policies. The meeting time policy (C13) is a concrete, observable practice. While these are anecdotal examples from one department, they are presented as factual descriptions rather than generalizable findings.

results.result: Access to childcare support varies significantly among women scientists in India. While some have access to family support and institutional childcare facilities, women living far from family face limited childcare options, particularly for infants. Hiring nannies is financially viable but many parents prefer childcare centers.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 describe disparities in childcare access based on expert opinion without systematic data on prevalence, geographic distribution, or economic factors. The assertion about parental preferences (C21) and financial viability (C20) lacks supporting evidence such as surveys or comparative cost analyses. Claims C16-C17 are specific factual statements about one individual's situation.

results.result: Mayurika Lahiri led a six-year effort to establish an on-campus childcare center at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research in Pune, which now serves 50 children. The institute provided space and startup funds, while parent fees cover operating expenses. The center provides peace of mind and allows parents to concentrate on work.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C34 provide specific, verifiable details about the establishment and operation of a childcare facility, including timeline (C26), capacity (C23), funding model (C29-C30), and governance structure (C27-C28). These are concrete, factual statements about a documented institutional initiative with specific outcomes.

results.result: Outdated institutional policies hinder women's careers in science, with a key challenge being insufficient women in decision-making positions to change attitudes. Despite this, senior women faculty are actively advocating for solutions to career challenges faced by mothers.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 present broad assertions about systemic problems without specific evidence of which policies are outdated or quantitative data on women's representation in leadership. Claim C37 describes advocacy efforts but lacks details about specific actions taken, their scope, or measurable outcomes beyond the examples that follow.

results.result: Maria Thaker's tenure application was evaluated by an all-male panel that did not account for her six-month maternity leave and compared her against a male colleague with more publications, resulting in a three-year contract extension instead of tenure. She was the first woman evaluated under a new tenure process.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 provide specific, factual details about a documented tenure case including the composition of the evaluation panel (C41), the comparison made (C42), and the outcome (C43). These are verifiable statements about a specific institutional decision, though they represent a single case study.

results.result: Following Thaker's case, Visweswariah and colleagues successfully lobbied for an institute-wide tenure clock policy allowing women faculty to pause the clock for one year per child (maximum two years), with retroactive application of tenure and pay increases. The policy accounts for maternity leave and post-return adjustment periods that male colleagues often fail to understand.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 describe a specific policy change with concrete details about implementation (C45), retroactive benefits (C46), and scope (C47). This represents a documented institutional policy reform with clear parameters. Claims C48-C49 provide rationale based on expert opinion about adjustment periods.

results.result: Women scientists across India are advocating for family-friendly policies including breastfeeding facilities and dual-career hiring. Experts suggest that government-mandated policies across all funded institutions would accelerate progress and prevent redundant policy development at each institution.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 describes ongoing advocacy efforts without specific examples, quantification of scope, or documentation of outcomes. Claims C51-C52 present speculative opinions about potential government intervention without evidence that such mandates would be effective or analysis of implementation challenges.

results.result: Supportive communities of colleagues, both domestic and international, help women scientists persist through administrative challenges. Thaker's experience demonstrates that colleague support was crucial in motivating her to overcome tenure-related obstacles.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by Thaker's direct testimony (C54) about the impact of colleague support on her decision-making. While this represents a single case and the broader claim (C53) about community support helping women generally is more inferential, the specific example is well-documented.
